claim: Nature brings immeasurable complexity at every conceivable level of organization, including ecological communities, populations, cell behavior, and gene regulation.
source: Nature brings us immeasurable complexity at every conceivable level of organization — ecological communities are composed of interacting networks of dynamically evolving players; populations of species are defined by membership in closely interacting groups competing for shared resources; cell behavior is governed by a myriad of overlapping and intertwined biochemical pathways and cell-cell interactions; gene regulation is carried out by a web of interacting transcription factors, modified by the cellular environment and epigenetic landscape.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the complexity observed in biological systems at multiple organizational levels.

claim: The study of biology has been organized into two distinct pursuits: 'How do things work?' (function) and 'How did they get that way?' (evolutionary history).
source: The first key level of simplification has been to separate function from evolutionary history, and to organize the study of biology into these two distinct pursuits: 'How do things work?' and 'How did they get that way?'.
evidence: This describes the historical organization of biological inquiry into functional and evolutionary domains.

claim: Functional biology simplifies systems by isolating organisms from their environmental context using lab-bred model organisms.
source: In the pursuit of functional understanding, the next step has been to simplify the system by isolating the organism from its environmental context. The tool of the trade is a lab-bred model organism — reared on defined growth media, isolated from its natural biotic and abiotic environments, stripped of its natural genetic heterozygosity, and removed from daily and seasonal fluctuations.
evidence: This describes the standard methodological approach in functional biology.

claim: Humanized mouse models serve as a canonical example of reducing biological system complexity by isolating individual components.
source: Humanized mouse models — specialized pure-breeding lines carrying human genes, cells, tissues, or organs — serve as a canonical example of the quest to reduce the complexity of a biological system by isolating its individual components.
evidence: This provides a specific example of the reductionist approach in functional biology.

claim: Evolutionary biology achieves simplification by separating the study of processes acting on populations over ecological timescales from consequences revealed on phylogenetic timescales.
source: It is achieved in a different way, however, by separating the study of processes acting on populations over ecological timescales from the consequences of these processes as revealed on phylogenetic timescales.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach to simplification in evolutionary biology.

claim: The separation of ecological and evolutionary timescales has been justified by the belief that ecological change can be rapid whereas evolutionary change is slow and gradual.
source: This separation of timescales has been justified by the belief that ecological change can be rapid — wildfires are an extreme example — whereas evolutionary change in response to an ecological challenge, such as increasingly frequent occurrence of wildfire, is a slow and gradual process.
evidence: This explains the rationale behind the separation of ecological and evolutionary studies.

claim: The human body is an entire ecosystem of interacting species and evolving somatic lineages.
source: Even our own human body is, in fact, an entire ecosystem of interacting species and evolving somatic lineages (Ley et al., 2006; Martincorena, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on the human microbiome and somatic evolution.

claim: As biological entities evolve, the network of their interactions also evolves.
source: As each of these multiple entities evolves, so too does the network of their interactions (e.g. Fiegna et al., 2015; Urban and Skelly, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating co-evolution of interactions.

claim: Function in biological systems is intimately linked to eco-evolutionary dynamics.
source: Function in these systems is intimately linked to eco-evolutionary dynamics and the eco-evolutionary dynamics are, of course, intimately linked to function.
evidence: This is a theoretical assertion about the relationship between function and eco-evolutionary dynamics.

claim: There is no separation of timescales between ecological and evolutionary processes.
source: There is no separation of timescales, just as there is no separation of the fields of inquiry.
evidence: This is an assertion that challenges the traditional view of separated timescales.

claim: Stripping experimental systems from their essential eco-evolutionary context can make functional insights positively misleading.
source: Indeed, stripping experimental systems from their essential eco-evolutionary context not only makes the resulting functional insights less relevant, it can make them positively misleading.
evidence: This is an argument about the consequences of decontextualized research.

claim: Recent advances in high-throughput measurement and high-performance computing enable interrogation of biological systems in their fuller eco-evolutionary context.
source: Instead, we argue that specifically now, with the recent advances in high-throughput measurement and high-performance computing, we might finally be in a position to interrogate biological systems in their fuller eco-evolutionary context, with the goal of exposing the hidden regularities and arrive at an emergent simplicity of understanding.
evidence: This is an assertion about current technological capabilities enabling new research approaches.

claim: Approximately 35% of genes in E. coli have no known function.
source: The fact that approximately 35% of genes in E. coli, perhaps the best studied organism in the lab, have no known function (Ghatak et al., 2019) is certainly not due to lack of effort, but speaks to the difficulty of understanding organisms in isolation.
evidence: This is a specific statistic cited from published research.

claim: The function of genes that are recalcitrant to mutational knockout analysis in the laboratory can be revealed under their natural biotic conditions.
source: The function of genes that are recalcitrant to mutational knockout analysis in the laboratory can be revealed under their natural biotic conditions (Barbaric et al., 2007; Chanin et al., 2019; Cruz et al., 2016; Hutchison et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2020; Richter et al., 2009; Ruff et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating context-dependent gene function.

claim: When Arabidopsis thaliana is grown in natural conditions, GWAS experiments reveal that natural variation in flowering is largely due to variation in circadian clock genes.
source: However, when this same species is grown in natural conditions, GWAS experiments reveal that natural variation in flowering is in fact largely due to variation in circadian clock genes (Brachi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited GWAS study.

claim: Selective breeding programs performed in one environment fail to improve the yield of crops grown in another environment.
source: It should therefore not be surprising that selective breeding programs performed in one environment fail to improve the yield of crops grown in another environment (Barrero Farfan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a cited observation about the context-dependence of breeding programs.

claim: There is difficulty in transferring polygenic scores in human GWAS across different contexts.
source: In these and many other examples, such as the difficulty of transferring polygenic scores in human GWAS (e.g. Rosenberg et al., 2019), the context matters enough that it changes the answer in entirely practical ways.
evidence: This is a cited example of context-dependent genetic effects in humans.

claim: Microorganisms often require the presence of their ecological partners in order to grow.
source: For instance, microorganisms often require the presence of their ecological partners in order to grow, a suggestion that was made at the dawn of microbiology (Winogradsky, 1935).
evidence: This is a historical observation cited from early microbiology.

claim: In low-diversity enrichment communities formed in minimal media, the metabolic activities of all co-occurring species dramatically transform the shared environment, permitting the growth of taxa that would otherwise be excluded.
source: This is true even for low-diversity enrichment communities formed in minimal media, where the metabolic activities of all co-occurring species dramatically transform the shared environment, thus permitting the growth of taxa that would otherwise be excluded (Estrela et al., 2020; Goldford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from cited experimental studies on microbial communities.

claim: The ability to isolate and cultivate soil bacteria is dramatically enhanced by embedding culture chambers in soil.
source: Studies have also found that our ability to isolate and cultivate soil bacteria is dramatically enhanced by embedding culture chambers in soil, further emphasizing the challenges that exist when we separate an individual species from its biotic context (Chaudhary et al., 2019; Kaeberlein et al., 2002; Nichols et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on bacterial cultivation methods.

claim: Many human pathogens only become virulent when in the company of other community members.
source: There is growing evidence, for example, that many human pathogens only become virulent when in the company of other community members (Hajishengallis and Lamont, 2016; Wiles and Guillemin, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from cited research on pathogen virulence.

claim: Mycorrhizal fungi rely on associated bacteria in order to provide services to their host plants.
source: In a similar vein, mycorrhizal fungi rely on associated bacteria in order to provide services to their host plants (Minerdi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study on mycorrhizal symbiosis.

claim: Host-pathogen dynamics in Arabidopsis thaliana are driven by a diffuse web of many interactions, including co-occurring host species sharing interacting pathogen species.
source: But, yet again, careful dissection of these interactions in Arabidopsis thaliana has revealed that these host-pathogen dynamics are driven by a diffuse web of many interactions, including co-occurring host species sharing interacting pathogen species (Karasov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study on host-pathogen interactions.

claim: Humans who live in regions of high pathogen diversity carry alleles with a broader efficacy.
source: For example, an investigation of the evolution of immunity has revealed that humans who live in regions of high pathogen diversity carry alleles with a broader efficacy, as has also been predicted by theory (Manczinger et al., 2019; Nourmohammad et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from cited empirical and theoretical studies on human immunity.

claim: In multispecies microbial consortia, important community functions are often the result of higher-than-pairwise functional interactions.
source: In multispecies microbial consortia, important community functions are often the result of higher-than-pairwise functional interactions (Sanchez-Gorostiaga et al., 2019), and the evolution of species traits is tightly constrained by the network of interactions with co-evolving species (Lawrence et al., 2012; Scheuerl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on microbial community interactions.

claim: The evolution of species traits is tightly constrained by the network of interactions with co-evolving species.
source: In multispecies microbial consortia, important community functions are often the result of higher-than-pairwise functional interactions (Sanchez-Gorostiaga et al., 2019), and the evolution of species traits is tightly constrained by the network of interactions with co-evolving species (Lawrence et al., 2012; Scheuerl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on co-evolution.

claim: Disease pressure on host species in a grassland community is predicted not only by the abundance of the host species but also by the phylogenetic diversity of the entire plant community.
source: For example, Parker et al., 2015 found that disease pressure on host species of a grassland community were predicted not only by the abundance of the one host species of interest, a phenomenon that is predictable by two-species models, but also by the phylogenetic diversity of the entire plant community.
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study on disease dynamics in plant communities.

claim: Negative frequency-dependent competition amongst strains of malaria and the selection that follows establish a pattern of limiting similarity that makes the community more robust to perturbations.
source: One recent, compelling example revealed that negative frequency-dependent competition amongst strains of malaria, and the selection that follows from this competition, establish a pattern of limiting similarity that makes the community more robust to perturbations (He et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study on malaria strain dynamics.

claim: Ecological and evolutionary processes jointly determine community resilience in malaria.
source: This demonstrates how ecological and evolutionary processes jointly determine community resilience, an important aspect of community function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the malaria study about the joint role of ecology and evolution.

claim: Interventions to control malaria must be more prolonged than currently implemented.
source: In this example, the applied relevance is clear - interventions to control malaria must be more prolonged than currently implemented.
evidence: This is an inference about practical implications drawn from the malaria study.

claim: Cancer is a process of the evolution of competing somatic lineages.
source: The relevance of eco-evolutionary dynamics is especially clear when we consider cancer, which we now understand to be a process of the evolution of competing somatic lineages.
evidence: This reflects current scientific understanding of cancer as an evolutionary process.

claim: Cancer dynamics depend on the ecological dynamics of complex cellular communities inside the body, involving interactions among multiple cell types.
source: Cancer dynamics depend in crucial ways on the ecological dynamics of the complex cellular communities inside the body, involving interactions and cross signaling among multiple dividing, dying and differentiating cell types such as stroma, tumor, and immune cells (Rodrigues et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a cited description of cancer as an ecological process.

claim: Targeted cancer therapies impact tumor growth by affecting not just the tumor cells but also the immune system.
source: We also know now that even targeted cancer therapies impact tumor growth by affecting not just the tumor cells but also the immune system (Deng et al., 2018; Goel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on cancer therapy mechanisms.

claim: Cancer therapies aimed at the immune system work very differently depending on the genotype of the tumor.
source: The same is true for the cancer therapies aimed at the immune system that work very differently depending on the genotype of the tumor (Song et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study on immunotherapy effectiveness.

claim: The etiology of many viral diseases is at its core an eco-evolutionary process that connects evolutionary dynamics of large viral populations to the shifting ecological landscape of the immune system.
source: Similarly, the etiology of many viral diseases is at its core an eco-evolutionary process that connects evolutionary dynamics of large viral populations to the shifting ecological landscape of the immune system.
evidence: This is a conceptual characterization of viral disease etiology.

claim: The ability of HIV to evolve sufficiently quickly to outrun the immune system and maintain resistance is the function that causes the disease of immune deficiency.
source: The ability of HIV to evolve sufficiently quickly to outrun the immune system and maintain resistance is not the context of function - it is function, at least in the sense that this is what causes the disease of immune deficiency.
evidence: This is an assertion about HIV pathogenesis based on established knowledge.

claim: The ability of viruses to jump from one species to another, evolve an ability to infect, and then spread is responsible for shutting down the economies of the whole world.
source: Along these same lines, the ability of viruses to jump from one species to another, evolve an ability to infect, and then spread, is currently responsible for shutting down the economies of the whole world.
evidence: This refers to the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic impact.

claim: Complexity at one level of organization does not preclude simplicity of explanation at a higher level.
source: First, complexity at one level of organization in no way precludes simplicity of explanation at a higher level.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle about emergent properties.

claim: Simplicity is always emergent in biological systems.
source: In fact, microscopically, all biological systems are impossibly complex. Predictable properties can only arise at some higher levels of organization: that is, simplicity is always emergent.
evidence: This is a theoretical assertion about the nature of biological complexity.

claim: Exponential growth law of a population is a property of the entire population, not of any individual member.
source: Even something as 'trivial' as the exponential growth law of a population summarizes a tremendous complexity of microscopic processes of growth and reproduction. The exponential growth is not a property of any member of the population; it is a property of the entire population.
evidence: This is an example of an emergent property in population biology.

claim: The enzymatic kinetics of Michaelis and Menten are immeasurably simpler than the microscopic laws of quantum chemistry.
source: Similarly, the enzymatic kinetics of Michaelis and Menten are immeasurably simpler than the microscopic laws of quantum chemistry 'under the hood', and our description of cell physiology rarely invokes the latter.
evidence: This is an example of emergent simplicity in biochemistry.

claim: The simplicity of quantitative phenomenological growth laws has been 'a source of wonder and inspiration'.
source: At the next level of organization, the simplicity of quantitative phenomenological growth laws (Schaechter et al., 1958) has been 'a source of wonder and inspiration' (Scott and Hwa, 2011).
evidence: This is a cited observation about bacterial growth laws.

claim: Despite the immense underlying complexity of genetic and metabolic regulation, growth laws can be largely explained by a simple, coarse-grained argument of proteome allocation into ribosomal vs. non-ribosomal components.
source: Despite the immense underlying complexity of genetic and metabolic regulation, growth laws can be largely explained by a simple, coarse-grained argument of proteome allocation into ribosomal vs. non-ribosomal components (Basan et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a cited theoretical explanation for bacterial growth laws.

claim: Mendelian genetics was originally derived without requiring any knowledge of the molecular or cellular processes from which they emerge.
source: At higher levels of organization, organismal traits may be predicted from the laws of mendelian genetics, which were originally derived without requiring any knowledge of the molecular or cellular processes from which they emerge and well before we even knew that DNA was the molecular carrier of genetic information.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the development of genetics.

claim: No physiological or molecular knowledge is required to calculate genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, or the effects of drift and selection on allele frequency.
source: No physiological or molecular knowledge is required either to calculate genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, or the effects of drift and selection on allele frequency.
evidence: This is a statement about the independence of population genetics principles from molecular details.

claim: Fundamental results of population genetics describe emergent population-level properties, which lack meaning at the level of a single individual organism.
source: Importantly, these and other fundamental results of population genetics describe emergent population-level properties, which lack meaning at the level of a single individual organism.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the nature of population genetics.

claim: Throughout the history of biology, successes were never about simplifying away the complexity of a system, but about finding the appropriate coarse-graining.
source: Throughout the history of biology, our successes were never about simplifying away the complexity of a system, but about finding the appropriate coarse-graining.
evidence: This is a historical interpretation of scientific methodology in biology.

claim: The microbiomes of different individual bromeliad plants contain highly similar fractions of their metagenomes devoted to respiration, fermentation, methanogenesis, and other metabolic functions despite varying widely in the species they contain.
source: For instance, the microbiomes of different individual bromeliad plants contain highly similar fractions of their metagenomes devoted to respiration, fermentation, methanogenesis, and other metabolic functions despite varying widely in the species they contain (Louca et al., 2017; Louca et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on bromeliad microbiomes.

claim: Predictable, species-level compositions are not required for generating predictable dynamics at the level of metabolites.
source: A logical conclusion from this observation is that predictable, species-level compositions are not required for generating predictable dynamics at the level of metabolites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bromeliad microbiome observations.

claim: Emergent simplicity arises generically in consumer-resource models.
source: Such emergent simplicity arises generically in consumer-resource models (Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019), and it is also exhibited by enrichment communities assembled in simple synthetic environments, where ecological sources of variation (e.g. migration, abiotic factors, bottlenecks, etc.) can be controlled (Estrela et al., 2020; Goldford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from cited theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: In minimal sugar-limited environments, two dominant metabolic groups are consistently found: respiro-fermentative bacteria that metabolize the sugar, and respirative bacteria that specialize on organic acids secreted by the former.
source: In minimal sugar-limited environments, for example, two dominant metabolic groups are consistently found: One group is made by respiro-fermentative bacteria, which metabolize the lion's share of the sugar, while the second group is made by respirative bacteria, which specialize on the organic acids that are secreted as overflow metabolic byproducts by the former.
evidence: This is a description of observed metabolic organization in microbial communities.

claim: The ratios of cell counts in each of the two metabolic groups are quantitatively consistent across communities that were started from different species pools.
source: The ratios of cell counts in each of these two metabolic groups are quantitatively consistent across communities that were started from different species pools in this system (Estrela et al., 2020; Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from cited experimental studies on microbial communities.

claim: A similar metabolic organization has been found to repeatedly arise in experimental evolution studies that started from a single isogenic strain.
source: A similar metabolic organization has been found to repeatedly arise in experimental evolution studies that started from a single isogenic strain (Good et al., 2017; Rozen and Lenski, 2000; Treves et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a finding from cited experimental evolution studies.

claim: After 700 generations in a glucose-limited chemostat, an initially isogenic population of E. coli had diversified into an ecosystem composed of four derived strains, with one strain adapted by increasing glucose uptake rate and others specialized in increased overflow metabolic secretions.
source: For instance, Rosenzweig and colleagues (Kinnersley et al., 2009; Rosenzweig et al., 1994) found that after only 700 generations in a glucose-limited chemostat, an initially isogenic population of E. coli had diversified into an ecosystem composed of four derived strains. One strain had adapted by increasing the rate of glucose uptake, while the others had specialized in the increased overflow metabolic secretions of the glucose specialist.
evidence: This is a specific finding from cited experimental evolution studies.

claim: Both top-down selection among a diverse pool of taxa and bottom-up community assembly via evolution from a single genotype lead to communities that predictably assemble into convergent functional structures.
source: We highlight this example because it demonstrates elegantly that both top-down selection among a diverse pool of taxa and bottom-up community assembly via evolution from a single genotype lead to communities that predictably assemble into convergent functional structures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental evolution and community assembly studies.

claim: This reproducibility can be explained from a metabolic tradeoff that is fundamentally conserved across all kingdoms of life, where fast-growth in sugars is associated with the secretion of overflow metabolites into the environment.
source: This reproducibility can be explained from a metabolic tradeoff that is fundamentally conserved across all kingdoms of life, where fast-growth in sugars is associated with the secretion of overflow metabolites into the environment.
evidence: This is an explanation based on fundamental metabolic principles.

claim: The amount of overflow byproducts produced per unit glucose consumed is governed by the glucose uptake rate: the faster a bacterium metabolizes glucose, the larger the amount of byproducts it releases.
source: The amount of these byproducts produced per unit glucose consumed is governed by the glucose uptake rate: the faster a bacterium metabolizes glucose, the larger the amount of byproducts it releases (Basan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a cited finding about bacterial metabolism.

claim: There is a tight covariation between glucose uptake rate and overflow metabolite production, even for isolates that belong to different genera.
source: This leads to a tight covariation between the magnitude of both, even for isolates that belong to different genera (Estrela et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a cited finding about metabolic relationships across bacterial taxa.

claim: Genome-scale metabolic models can correctly estimate the ratio of both metabolic groups by making simple assumptions.
source: Genome-scale metabolic models can correctly estimate the ratio of both metabolic groups by making such simple assumptions.
evidence: This is a statement about the predictive power of metabolic models.

claim: Predictability in microbial communities is enabled by the fact that metabolism is highly structured, only some solutions are sensible or mathematically possible, and bacterial taxa have been coevolving with each other for eons.
source: In these examples, predictability was enabled by the fact that metabolism is highly structured, only some solutions are sensible or mathematically possible, and bacterial taxa have been coevolving with each other for eons, making microbial communities very nonrandom.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed predictability in microbial systems.

claim: Biochemical, physiological, and physical constraints, combined with (co)evolution, might often lead to predictable and understandable outcomes in other microbial and non-microbial systems.
source: In a similar way, biochemical, physiological, and physical constraints, combined with (co)evolution, might often lead to predictable and, hence, potentially understandable outcomes in other microbial and non-microbial systems.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization from microbial systems to other biological systems.

claim: Co-adaptation and co-evolution, especially when it comes to functionally important community or individual traits, will be governed by a limited number of driving forces that will allow for a simpler coarse-grained understanding to emerge.
source: It is our contention and hope that co-adaptation and co-evolution, especially when it comes to functionally important community or individual traits, will be governed by a limited number of driving forces that, when revealed, will allow for a simpler coarse-grained understanding to emerge.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the nature of biological complexity.

claim: The limitations of a reductionist approach are well established.
source: This is not the conversation we are trying to have: the limitations of a reductionist approach are well established, as is the fact that the tremendous progress the biological sciences have experienced over the past centuries, both fundamental and applied, has been due almost entirely to this very approach.
evidence: This is a statement about the established understanding of reductionism in biology.

claim: The tremendous progress the biological sciences have experienced over the past centuries has been due almost entirely to the reductionist approach.
source: This is not the conversation we are trying to have: the limitations of a reductionist approach are well established, as is the fact that the tremendous progress the biological sciences have experienced over the past centuries, both fundamental and applied, has been due almost entirely to this very approach.
evidence: This is a historical assessment of the success of reductionism in biology.

claim: 'What the pieces do' may not be clear when the whole is extracted from its biological context.
source: First, we must remember that 'what the pieces do' may not be clear when the whole is extracted from its biological context.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about decontextualized research.

claim: When we design our experiments around simplified environments, it is not out of a belief that the natural context doesn't matter, but as a matter of feasibility.
source: When we design our experiments around simplified environments, it is not out of a belief that the natural context doesn't matter, but as a matter of feasibility.
evidence: This is an observation about the practical motivations for experimental simplification.

claim: The tools that we use shape the research that we do.
source: This is essential because the tools that we use shape the research that we do, and as we get better and better sequencing, for example, the comparative lack of tools for high-throughput phenotyping is becoming increasingly a problem.
evidence: This is a general principle about the relationship between methodology and research direction.

claim: The comparative lack of tools for high-throughput phenotyping is becoming increasingly a problem as sequencing technology improves.
source: This is essential because the tools that we use shape the research that we do, and as we get better and better sequencing, for example, the comparative lack of tools for high-throughput phenotyping is becoming increasingly a problem.
evidence: This is an observation about current technological limitations in biology.

claim: There is a danger of keeping to zoom in on the increasingly microscopic details of species in isolation, where the existing street lights shine brightest.
source: The danger is to keep zooming in on the increasingly microscopic details of species in isolation, where the existing street lights shine brightest.
evidence: This is a metaphorical warning about research bias toward available methods.

claim: New technology for high-throughput functional characterization of organisms in natural or semi-natural habitats of growing eco-evolutionary context is needed.
source: We therefore call for redoubling our efforts to develop new technology for high-throughput functional characterization of organisms in natural or semi-natural habitats of growing eco-evolutionary context (Mallard et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a call for technological development with a citation to related work.

claim: At the outset, we cannot know how much contextual richness is enough.
source: But how much is enough? At the outset, we cannot know.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty in experimental design.

claim: Model systems should be integrated into an axis of tunable contextual richness: lab, semi-natural, and natural.
source: Thus, we're advocating for model systems that can be integrated into an axis of tunable contextual richness: lab, semi-natural, and natural.
evidence: This is a proposed methodological approach.

claim: As we increase the size and complexity of experimental systems in a controlled manner, we will search for emergent properties that only reveal themselves at higher levels of organization.
source: As we increase the size and complexity of experimental systems in a controlled manner, we will search for emergent properties that only reveal themselves at higher levels of organization (and at the appropriate coarse-graining).
evidence: This is a proposed research strategy.

claim: We can attempt to search for emergent properties in a systematic manner, rather than discovering them by serendipity.
source: We can attempt to search for these emergent properties in a systematic manner, rather than discovering them by serendipity.
evidence: This is a proposed methodological improvement.

claim: A concerted effort to find emergent properties will benefit from looking across a diverse array of organisms because only then will consistent, and likely robust, emergent patterns become recognizable.
source: Such a concerted effort will benefit from looking across a diverse array of organisms because only then will consistent, and likely robust, emergent patterns become recognizable.
evidence: This is a proposed research strategy based on comparative approaches.

claim: This experimental methodology would go hand in hand with recent calls in theoretical literature for models of 'appropriate complexity'.
source: This experimental methodology would go hand in hand with the recent calls in theoretical literature for models of 'appropriate complexity' (Getz et al., 2018).
evidence: This connects the proposed approach to existing theoretical work.

claim: Finding the appropriate level of coarse-graining remains a matter of art, an art that becomes harder as systems become more complex.
source: Finding the appropriate level of coarse-graining remains a matter of art, an art that becomes harder and harder as the systems become more complex.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the difficulty in finding appropriate simplifications.

claim: Machine learning and AI methods for performing automated variable selection for learning sparse predictive models may prove effective in finding appropriate coarse-graining.
source: One exciting possibility is that machine learning and AI methods for performing automated variable selection for learning sparse predictive models will prove effective.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about the potential of AI methods.

claim: More data are not yet progress.
source: Just like more data are not yet progress, a bigger computer alone will not suffice: AI can discover phenomenological regularities, but for such regularities to clue us into underlying causal forces and guide our interrogation of biological systems, data-intensive approaches need to be integrated with the eco-evolutionary theory of functional biology.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the limitations of data alone.

claim: AI can discover phenomenological regularities, but for such regularities to clue us into underlying causal forces, data-intensive approaches need to be integrated with the eco-evolutionary theory of functional biology.
source: Just like more data are not yet progress, a bigger computer alone will not suffice: AI can discover phenomenological regularities, but for such regularities to clue us into underlying causal forces and guide our interrogation of biological systems, data-intensive approaches need to be integrated with the eco-evolutionary theory of functional biology.
evidence: This is an argument for integrating computational and theoretical approaches.

claim: Many of the most pressing problems facing humanity - from global change, to infectious disease and zoonosis, to cancer - are all problems of eco-evolutionary function.
source: Many of the most pressing problems facing humanity - from global change, to infectious disease and zoonosis, to cancer - are all problems of eco-evolutionary function.
evidence: This is a characterization of major societal challenges as eco-evolutionary problems.

claim: Confronting these problems will require that we build a sufficient understanding that we can predict, and even control, how these systems function as they evolve.
source: Confronting these problems will require that we build a sufficient understanding that we can predict, and even control, how these systems function as they evolve.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical requirements for addressing major challenges.

claim: These are challenging and crucial problems that will require concerted collaboration across currently disparate fields that extend much beyond the traditional boundaries of Ecology and Evolution.
source: These are challenging and yet crucial problems that will require concerted collaboration across currently disparate fields that extend much beyond the traditional boundaries of Ecology and Evolution, and include all branches of Organismal and Functional Biology, as well as Physics, Engineering, Statistics, and Computer Science.
evidence: This is a call for interdisciplinary collaboration.

claim: The enterprise of studying organisms in isolation and as static, already evolved entities, while hugely successful, is also profoundly limited.
source: As we have argued, the enterprise of studying organisms in isolation and as static, already evolved entities, while hugely successful, is also profoundly limited.
evidence: This is a summary assessment of traditional biological approaches.

claim: Much of what one learns about the functional behavior of E.coli in isolation hardly even extends to E.coli in the gut, let alone to elephants in the savannah.
source: Our belief, which lies in contrast to Jacques Monod's famous dictum — 'Anything found to be true of E. coli must also be true of elephants' — is that much of what one learns about the functional behavior of E.coli in isolation hardly even extends to E.coli in the gut, let alone to elephants in the savannah.
evidence: This is an assertion that challenges a famous principle in biology, based on the arguments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The creation of a new field of Function of Evolving Systems that focuses on the function of organisms in the communities in which they reside, over periods of time when interactions evolve, is both exciting intellectually and essential practically.
source: The heart of our proposal, here, is thus the creation of a new field of Function of Evolving Systems that focuses on the function of organisms in the communities in which they reside, over periods of time when interactions evolve. It is both exciting intellectually, and essential practically.
evidence: This is the central proposal of the manuscript.
